questions.stem: A client retries a failed HTTP request immediately and without limit. During a partial outage of the server, what is the most likely effect?
options: Retry traffic piles onto the struggling server and slows its recovery
Recovery speeds up because every client reaches the server sooner
Nothing changes, because the server cannot tell a retry from a request
Latency drops for all callers as soon as the outage begins

rationale.overall: Unbounded immediate retries multiply load on a dependency that is already failing, which is why retries are normally capped and spaced out with backoff and jitter.
options: Correct: retries add load exactly when the server has the least capacity to absorb it
Reaching an overloaded server sooner does not help it recover; it adds to the queue
The server does see every retry as additional work, whether or not it can label it
Extra load during an outage raises latency rather than lowering it

questions.tip: Pair retries with a cap, exponential backoff and jitter.

questions.stem: A schema migration failed halfway through and must be run again. Which property of its steps makes a re-run safe?
options: Each step is scheduled for a quiet hour of the day
Each step is idempotent, so repeating it changes nothing
Each step is written inside one very large comment block
Each step raises the statement timeout before it starts

rationale.overall: An idempotent step produces the same end state whether it runs once or several times, so a partial run can simply be repeated.
options: Timing reduces user impact but does not make a repeated step safe
Correct: idempotent steps can be re-applied after a partial failure without harm
Commented-out SQL does not run at all, so it migrates nothing
A longer timeout changes how long a step may run, not whether repeating it is safe

questions.tip: Prefer create-if-not-exists and guarded updates in migrations.

questions.stem: A unit test passes on a laptop but fails now and then in continuous integration. What should be investigated first?
options: The CI machine renders fonts differently from the laptop
The name of the test is too long for the CI log viewer
Shared state or timing dependence between tests
The repository has accumulated too many old branches

rationale.overall: Intermittent failures that depend on the environment usually come from test order, shared mutable state or timing assumptions rather than cosmetic differences.
options: Font rendering rarely affects a unit test and would fail consistently, not now and then
A long test name affects display only and cannot change the outcome
Correct: order-dependent state and timing races are the classic source of flaky tests
Branch count has no effect on how a single test executes

questions.tip: Run the suite in random order to expose hidden coupling.

questions.stem: What does a code review gain when the change under review is small and has a single purpose?
options: It removes the need for any automated test coverage
It guarantees that the merged change contains no defects
It lets the author skip writing a description of the change
Reviewers can hold the whole change in mind and spot defects

rationale.overall: Small focused diffs fit in a reviewer's working memory, which improves how many defects a review catches.
options: Tests and review catch different problems; a small diff replaces neither
No review process can guarantee the absence of defects
Context still matters for reviewers and future readers, whatever the size
Correct: a focused change can be understood completely, so problems stand out

questions.tip: Split refactors from behaviour changes so each diff tells one story.

questions.stem: An agent calls a tool and the tool returns an error. What should the agent loop do with that result?
options: Return the error to the model as the tool result so it can adapt
Drop the call silently and continue with the next step
Restart the whole conversation from the very first message
Rewrite the error as a success so that the run can finish

rationale.overall: Feeding the error back lets the model correct its arguments, choose another tool or explain the failure, instead of acting on a result that never happened.
options: Correct: the model can only recover from an error it is allowed to see
Silently dropping the call hides the failure and leaves the model working from a false picture
Restarting discards useful progress and will usually hit the same error again
Reporting a failure as a success causes the agent to act on results that do not exist

questions.tip: Treat tool errors as information for the model, not exceptions to hide.

questions.stem: Why should every tool exposed to an agent have a precise name and description?
options: Descriptions are read only by the people who maintain the tools
The model decides which tool to call largely from that text
Longer tool names reduce the number of tokens in each request
A good description lets a tool run without any input schema

rationale.overall: The model sees tool names and descriptions when choosing what to call, so vague text leads directly to wrong or missed tool calls.
options: The model reads them too, and relies on them when choosing a tool
Correct: tool selection is driven by the name and description the model is given
Longer names add tokens rather than removing them
Descriptions explain purpose; the input schema still defines the arguments

questions.tip: Write tool descriptions for the model as carefully as for a teammate.

questions.stem: A long-running agent is close to filling its context window. Which approach keeps the most useful information?
options: Delete the oldest messages without reading what they contain
Raise the sampling temperature for the remaining turns
Summarise finished work and keep open decisions verbatim
Move to a model that has a smaller context window

rationale.overall: Compacting completed work into a summary frees space while the details that still matter, such as open decisions and constraints, are kept exactly.
options: Blind truncation can remove constraints the agent still needs
Temperature changes randomness, not how much context is available
Correct: summarise what is settled and preserve what is still in play
A smaller window makes the space problem worse, not better

questions.tip: Decide what must survive compaction before the window is full.

questions.stem: When should an agent hand a decision to a person instead of acting on its own?
options: Every single time one of its tool calls completes without an error
Never, because full autonomy is the purpose of an agent
Only once its context window has been completely used up
When an action is irreversible or beyond its granted authority

rationale.overall: Escalation is warranted when a mistake cannot be undone or when the action exceeds what the agent was authorised to do.
options: Routine successful calls are exactly what an agent should handle alone
Useful agents still operate inside limits that people set
Context size is a resource issue, not a reason to escalate a decision
Correct: irreversible or out-of-scope actions are the points where people should decide

questions.tip: Define the escalation boundary up front, in the agent's instructions.
